questions.stem: A 31 year old man has thickened, nodular Achilles tendons noted by a physiotherapist treating his ankle sprain. His father had a myocardial infarction at 44. He does not smoke. His BMI is 23 kg/m². Investigations: total cholesterol 10.2 mmol/L (<5.0), LDL cholesterol 8.1 mmol/L (<3.0), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (<1.7), TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.4–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Very high LDL with normal triglycerides, tendon xanthomas and premature family CVD is familial hypercholesterolaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Tendon xanthomas plus very high LDL and a family history of early MI.

elim: Raises both cholesterol and triglycerides; tendon xanthomas are not typical.
TSH is normal.
No oedema or proteinuria is described.
Usually raises triglycerides and lowers HDL, with no tendon xanthomas.

steps.x: B. Familial hypercholesterolaemia. Very high cholesterol + tendon xanthomas = FH until proven otherwise; assess urgently.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has an NHS Health Check. She feels well and has no symptoms. She eats a lot of takeaway food. Her BMI is 31 kg/m² and BP 132/84 mmHg. There are no skin or tendon abnormalities.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised LDL and triglycerides found incidentally on routine bloods in an asymptomatic woman is hyperlipidaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

BP is below 140/90 mmHg.
HbA1c is normal so diabetes is excluded.
No oedema or proteinuria.

steps.x: B. Hyperlipidaemia. Hyperlipidaemia is usually asymptomatic and found on a lipid profile.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman is concerned about painless, soft yellow plaques on the medial aspect of both upper eyelids that have slowly grown over a year. Her vision is normal. She has no other symptoms. Her BMI is 28 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood tests?
questions.e: Xanthelasma are cholesterol deposits around the eyelids and suggest raised LDL cholesterol.

Yellow eyelid plaques are xanthelasma.

Iron overload causes bronzing, not xanthelasma.
Gout gives tophi on ears and joints, not eyelid plaques.

steps.x: C. Raised LDL cholesterol. Xanthelasma: think lipids; check a full lipid profile.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a total cholesterol of 7.9 mmol/L at a routine check; it was 5.2 mmol/L three years ago. She has gained 6 kg, feels cold and has a hoarse voice. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm. Her reflexes are slow-relaxing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised cholesterol?
questions.e: New hypercholesterolaemia with cold intolerance, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes is a reversible secondary cause: hypothyroidism.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her raised cholesterol? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A new rise in cholesterol plus classic hypothyroid features.

Cholesterol was normal 3 years ago; FH is present from birth.
No oedema or frothy urine.
Can raise cholesterol but presents with itch and cholestatic LFTs.

steps.x: C. Hypothyroidism. Always check TFTs: hypothyroidism is a reversible cause.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has a week of swelling around his eyes in the morning and swollen ankles. His urine is frothy. His BP is 98/60 mmHg. Investigations: serum albumin 18 g/L (35–50), urine protein:creatinine ratio 650 mg/mmol (<15), total cholesterol 8.9 mmol/L (<5.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hyperlipidaemia?
questions.e: Proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia make up nephrotic syndrome.

Periorbital oedema, frothy urine and low albumin are nephrotic.

Does not cause oedema or proteinuria.

Not suggested; he has oedema, not obesity.

steps.x: D. Nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is associated with hyperlipidaemia.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with familial hypercholesterolaemia stopped his statin years ago. He has 3 months of central chest tightness when walking uphill that eases within 5 minutes of rest. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. His resting ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Untreated FH accelerates atherosclerosis, causing ischaemic heart disease; exertional pain relieved by rest is stable angina.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Untreated very high LDL plus classic exertional angina.

elim: Tearing pain at rest radiating to the back, not exertional.
Related to meals and lying, not exertion.
Sharp pain relieved by sitting forward.
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness.

steps.x: E. Stable angina. The key complication of hyperlipidaemia is cardiovascular disease.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with untreated hyperlipidaemia (LDL 5.8 mmol/L) suddenly develops weakness of his right arm and face and difficulty finding words. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, regular, and BP 168/94 mmHg. Glucose is 6.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication of his hyperlipidaemia?
questions.e: Atherosclerosis from hyperlipidaemia and smoking causes stroke; sudden arm/face weakness and dysphasia fits a left MCA infarct.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely complication of his hyperlipidaemia? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Sudden focal deficit in a man with major atherosclerotic risk factors.

elim: Affects the whole face only, with no arm weakness or dysphasia.
Glucose is normal.
Gradual, with headache, in younger patients.
Gradual onset after trauma, often with confusion.

steps.x: C. Ischaemic stroke. Hyperlipidaemia → atherosclerosis → IHD and stroke.

questions.stem: A GP reviews a 44 year old man with LDL cholesterol 4.9 mmol/L. He has no xanthomas and no family history of early heart disease. He drinks 10 units a week. His HbA1c and TSH are normal. His BMI is 34 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely contributing factor to his hyperlipidaemia?
questions.e: With secondary causes excluded, obesity and poor diet are the common risk factors.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely contributing factor to his hyperlipidaemia? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

TSH is normal.
No proteinuria or oedema.
HbA1c is normal.

steps.x: D. Obesity and diet. Risk factors: poor diet, obesity, diabetes, smoking.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a lipid profile showing triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L (<1.7), HDL 0.8 mmol/L (>1.0) and LDL 3.6 mmol/L (<3.0). He has had thirst and nocturia for 3 months. His BMI is 33 kg/m². TSH is normal. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+.
questions.q: Which is the most likely secondary cause of his lipid profile?
questions.e: Thirst, nocturia and glycosuria suggest diabetes, a secondary cause of hyperlipidaemia (high triglycerides, low HDL).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely secondary cause of his lipid profile? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Osmotic symptoms plus glycosuria = diabetes.

Mainly raised LDL with normal triglycerides.
TSH is normal.
Dipstick shows glucose, not protein.

steps.x: E. Type 2 diabetes. Secondary causes: diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman's total cholesterol is 8.6 mmol/L at a new patient check. Her mother started a statin at 30 and her uncle died suddenly at 41. She has no xanthomas. TSH, HbA1c and LFTs are normal. Her BMI is 22 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Total cholesterol above 7.5 mmol/L with premature CVD in relatives should prompt assessment for FH even without xanthomas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Cholesterol above 7.5, young, lean, strong family history.

TSH is normal.
No oedema or proteinuria.
LFTs are normal.

steps.x: A. Familial hypercholesterolaemia. TC >7.5 mmol/L → investigate for FH.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has membranous nephropathy with heavy proteinuria and serum albumin of 21 g/L. His total cholesterol has risen to 9.4 mmol/L. His TSH is normal. A student asks why his cholesterol rose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Loss of LDL in the urine
Reduced LDL receptor expression from hypothyroidism

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Nephrotic picture; thyroid excluded.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man is seen in a lipid clinic after a routine blood test showed LDL cholesterol 7.6 mmol/L with normal triglycerides. He has no symptoms and does not smoke. His father had a coronary bypass at 50 and his sister takes a statin. His BMI is 24 kg/m² and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Tendon xanthomas, typically at the Achilles and finger extensor tendons, are characteristic of FH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Very high LDL, family history: FH.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with no cardiovascular disease has a fasting lipid profile. Investigations: total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L (<5.0), HDL cholesterol 1.6 mmol/L (>1.2), LDL cholesterol 4.1 mmol/L (<3.0), triglycerides 1.5 mmol/L (<1.7). She asks how much her cholesterol matters.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with no cardiovascular disease has a total cholesterol of 6.1 mmol/L. He smokes and has treated hypertension. He asks whether he needs a statin. His BP is 136/82 mmHg. His BMI is 29 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to guide treatment?

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a total cholesterol of 7.2 mmol/L. She has gained weight, has heavy periods and her hair is thinning. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm. Before deciding on lipid treatment, the GP wants to exclude a reversible cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of hypercholesterolaemia and should be excluded with TFTs.

Hypothyroid features.

elim: Checked if a statin causes muscle symptoms.
Not routinely used.

steps.x: D. Thyroid function tests. Exclude secondary causes: HbA1c, TFTs, LFTs.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with QRISK3 of 15% agrees to start atorvastatin 20 mg. He drinks 30 units of alcohol a week. His BP is 134/82 mmHg. He has had a lipid profile, HbA1c and TFTs.
questions.q: Which other investigation is needed before starting the statin?
questions.e: LFTs are checked before starting a statin (and his alcohol use adds risk).

steps.x: The question asks: Which other investigation is needed before starting the statin? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Lipids and TFTs done; LFTs remain.

elim: Has no role before starting a statin.
Only if muscle symptoms or risk factors.
Not needed for primary prevention.
Not a pre-statin requirement.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman started atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention. She has no side effects. Her baseline non-HDL cholesterol was 5.0 mmol/L. She asks when her bloods will be repeated.
questions.q: When should her lipid profile and LFTs be repeated?
questions.e: Lipids and LFTs are repeated at 3 months to check a ≥40% non-HDL reduction and liver safety.

steps.x: The question asks: When should her lipid profile and LFTs be repeated? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
New statin needs follow-up.

elim: Too early for effect.
Far too late.
Misses early LFT changes and non-response.
Monitoring is required.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a total cholesterol of 8.1 mmol/L on a single test ordered by an occupational health service. He is asymptomatic and does not smoke. His brother had an MI at 49. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. No breakdown of the cholesterol result was reported.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A full lipid profile (TC, LDL, HDL, TG) is needed; TC >7.5 prompts FH assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
High TC with family history.

elim: Invasive; not the first step.
QRISK3 underestimates risk in FH.

TFTs, not imaging, exclude hypothyroidism.

steps.x: B. Full lipid profile. Full lipid profile; TC >7.5 → think FH.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a lipid profile at his GP showing triglycerides of 3.4 mmol/L (<1.7) and LDL 4.2 mmol/L (<3.0). He is overweight and reports 2 months of thirst and passing more urine at night. His BMI is 32 kg/m². TFTs and LFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate to exclude a secondary cause?
questions.e: HbA1c screens for diabetes, a secondary cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which investigation is most appropriate to exclude a secondary cause? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

steps.x: Thirst and weight suggest diabetes.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with no cardiovascular disease has a QRISK3 score of 13%. She has already improved her diet and exercise for 3 months. Her non-HDL cholesterol is 4.8 mmol/L. Her LFTs and TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Primary prevention with QRISK3 ≥10%: atorvastatin 20 mg, aiming >40% reduction in non-HDL.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Primary prevention above threshold.

Not first-line.
QRISK3 ≥10% justifies a statin.

steps.x: A. Atorvastatin 20 mg. Primary: atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK3 ≥10%.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 20 years has a total cholesterol of 4.6 mmol/L. He asks whether he needs a statin given his normal cholesterol. He has microalbuminuria. His BP is 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: No statin as cholesterol is normal
questions.e: In diabetes a statin is indicated regardless of baseline lipid levels.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Diabetes increases CV risk.

Not first-line.
Delays protection.

steps.x: B. Offer atorvastatin 20 mg. Diabetes: statin regardless of lipids.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is seen in the TIA clinic 2 weeks after 20 minutes of left arm weakness that fully resolved. He has no other history and takes no medication. His BP is 138/84 mmHg. His total cholesterol is 4.9 mmol/L, eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m² and LFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate lipid-lowering management?
o: No treatment as cholesterol is normal
questions.e: Established CVD (including TIA) needs high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg regardless of baseline lipids.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate lipid-lowering management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

steps.x: Secondary prevention.

elim: Primary prevention dose.
An add-on when a statin is insufficient, not first-line.
Secondary prevention is given regardless of baseline lipids.
Low intensity; established CVD needs high intensity.

steps.x: B. Atorvastatin 80 mg. Secondary prevention: atorvastatin 80 mg.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with chronic kidney disease has a QRISK3 of 22% and no history of cardiovascular disease. He agrees to start a statin. His BP is 136/80 mmHg. Investigations: eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m² (>90), ALT 22 U/L (<40), TSH 1.8 mU/L (0.4–4.0), total cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L (<5.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate statin dose?
questions.e: In CKD a lower dose (atorvastatin 20 mg) is used, increasing only if needed and eGFR allows.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate statin dose? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
CKD changes the dose.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolaemia after cascade testing because her father had an MI at 46. Her LDL is 6.9 mmol/L. She has no cardiovascular disease and no symptoms. She is not pregnant and uses contraception. Her LFTs and TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: High-intensity statin and lipid specialist referral
questions.e: FH: start a high-intensity statin promptly and refer to a lipid specialist.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
FH, young, very high LDL.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman started atorvastatin 20 mg 3 months ago (QRISK3 17%). Her non-HDL cholesterol has fallen from 5.2 to 4.4 mmol/L. She takes it every night and has no side effects. Her LFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

No side effects.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: If maximal statin is insufficient, add ezetimibe first.

Max statin, inadequate response.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia had a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
questions.e: PCSK9 inhibitors are second-line escalation when statin and ezetimibe are insufficient.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man attends an NHS Health Check. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, eats a diet high in saturated fat and rarely exercises. His BMI is 29 kg/m² and BP 132/82 mmHg. His total cholesterol is 6.0 mmol/L and his QRISK3 score is 7%.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Low risk; lifestyle.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with long-standing untreated hyperlipidaemia (LDL 5.4 mmol/L) dies of a myocardial infarction. questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has a lipid profile: total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 2.8 mmol/L and HDL 2.1 mmol/L. Her QRISK3 is 4%. She read that a high HDL is good for her heart and asks the practice nurse why it protects against heart disease.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl is tested after her father, aged 38, was found to have familial hypercholesterolaemia with tendon xanthomas. Her LDL is 6.8 mmol/L with normal triglycerides. Her mother's lipids are normal. Her paternal grandfather died of an MI aged 45.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with a QRISK3 of 14% has not reduced his cholesterol with 3 months of diet and exercise. His non-HDL cholesterol is 4.9 mmol/L. He starts atorvastatin 20 mg at night and asks the pharmacist how the tablet lowers his cholesterol.
